content.title: Improving access, engagement could boost RSV vaccination rates among older adults, researchers suggest
content.text: (Photo credit: Igor Barilo/Getty Images) Vaccination rates against respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, remain low among older adults. Improving access to vaccination services as well as consistent public health engagement could help boost older adults’ confidence in the vaccine and improve vaccination rates, according to a study published in Vaccine. By the end of 2024-25 respiratory virus season, 38.3% of adults aged 60 to 74 who were at increased risk of severe RSV, and 41.5% of those 75 and older had received an RSV vaccine, according to the study. Researchers found that factors associated with increased RSV vaccination included having a household income above the poverty level, having a college graduate or higher level of education, not having a disability, and receiving provider recommendation for RSV vaccination. The study examined data on about 64,000 adults surveyed September 2024 through April 2025 as part of the National Immunization Survey-Adult COVID Module. The investigators used the Kaplan−Meier survival analysis procedure to assess RSV vaccination coverage at national and state level. The results showed that among those who had ever received RSV vaccination, 56.2% of adults aged 60 to 74 years and 55.4% of adults aged 75 years or older reported receiving it before the start of the 2024–25 season. The vaccination rates also significantly varied between states, with rates of 10.8% in Virgin Islands to 61.2% in Michigan among adults aged 60 to 74 years at increased risk, as well as 7.2% in Virgin Islands to 57.6% in Colorado among adults aged 75 years or older. “RSV vaccination uptake was low, with disparities by race/ethnicity and other factors, as well as wide variation across states or territories,” the authors said. “Continual monitoring of RSV vaccination will be helpful for developing tailored strategies to improve vaccination coverage.”
